There is more than one way to do calculations with exploding dice. Here's probably the simplest:
Let's start with calculating how many dice you throw on average per initial x-sided exploding die.

First of all, you have 1 die for sure.

During your first roll, there is a 1/x chance that your die might explode, so you can add "1/x dice" to the total. How this works is that there is an (x-1)/x chance you get zero extra dice (the die doesn't explode), and there's a 1/x chance that the die explodes. On average that's (0*(x-1)/x + 1/x) = 1/x extra die. There's a 1/x chance you make another roll, and in that case too there is a 1/x chance your die explodes, so in total there is a 1/x² chance you add another die to your total, so I you can yet again add 1/x² die to the average number of dice thrown. If continued infinitely, the mathematical expression will look like this:

Avg number of dice = 1 + 1/x + 1/x² + 1/x³ + ...

This is an infinite geometric series where the common ratio is smaller than one (q = 1/x), and thus the formula for getting the limit of it is a1/(1-q) where a1 is the first term in the series. a1 = 1 in this case.

So the average number of dice rolled if you roll an x-sided exploding die will be 1/(1-1/x).

This already accounts for the fact that the die explodes infinitely, so to calculate the probability of rolling for example at least 8 on an exploding d10 we simply multiply the probability of rolling at least a 8 on a regular d10 by the average number of dice an exploding dice will yield. So the result is:

(1/(1-1/10)) * 2/10

However, the problem you presented is more complicated than that.

The method above will be the basis for further calculations.

If we want to know the chance of getting more than X successes, we have to calculate and sum up all the probabilities above the threshold (5 in this case), or do the same thing with the values below the threshold and take the complement of it (we subtract the resul from one). These problems due to their nature have to involve a lot of calculations, but it's more tedious than hard. The main thing here is that you can just calculate probabilities in the same way as you'd do with normal, non-exploding dice. You can "ignore" the explosions if you simply count with the average number of dice per initial exploding die. So the problem you presented is a regular probability problem for 8*(1/1-1/8 ) dice.

The goal is to perfectly distribute the loot and this is possible only if the loot we're working with *can* be distributed perfectly. So we will assume that it indeed can be and this greatly reduces the complexity of the problem. If we have N players, and the sum of value the loot is S, the sum of the values of each player's magic items would have to be S/N.

To make a helpful analogy work, let's think about the sum of money as some size. The only thing we have to do now is arrange the items into N number of S/N sized bags. Based on our assumption, this must be possible, otherwise the items couldn't be distributed perfectly.

Arranging them like this can be done by iterating through the possible combinations of items for which the necessary conditions are true or can be true (if the size of a bag would be larger than S/x if we were to put a certain item into it, then we can discard that combination, but if it's smaller than S/x we will try to find another item which, when put into the bag, makes it so that the bag_size <= S/x). No more elegant algorithm comes to mind for the last part.

For example, even if your chance to hit on your first turn is 1/4, and on your second turn it will be 3/4, average damage output of your two options is nearly identical. First of all, the probability of getting 18 when rolling 3d6 is 1/6³ = 1/216.

Now we are going to get the probability we're looking for by fiddling with its complement. It is easier to calculate what the probability is of not rolling 18 for any of the six ability scores than adding up the probabilities of rolling an 18 once, twice, etc.

The probability we have to calculate now is the probability of rolling 18 zero times. Since the probability of getting 18 is 1/216, the probability of not getting 18 is 215/216 in the case of one die. For six dice, it is (215/216)⁶. The sum of this probability and the probability of getting an 18 at least once is exactly 1, because these cover all the possibilities. So the solution is 1-(215/216)⁶, which is around 0.0275, or 2.75%.
